analysis.file_name: Bernstein - U.S. Data Center Capacity - Your seat is skewing your numbers. Five ways to forecast DC capacity (and our definitive view).pdf
analysis.title: U.S. Data Center Capacity: Your seat is skewing your numbers. Five ways to forecast DC capacity (and our definitive view)
key_insights: A survey of 63 forecasts from 40 sources puts U.S. data center capacity in 2030 anywhere from 59 to 186 GW. Bernstein attributes the spread to starting assumptions, measurement units, timing conventions and where the forecaster sits in the value chain, not to disagreement on end demand.

Bernstein's definitive estimate is 149 IT-GW of U.S. capacity by 2030 (Exhibit 1: 33.7 in 2025, 47.3 in 2026E, 67.0 in 2027E, 92.4 in 2028E, 120.5 in 2029E, 149.2 in 2030E). It adds 19 IT-GW (~25 facility GW) in 2027 and 25 IT-GW (~32 facility GW) in 2028.
The PM Summary says the most reasonable outcome is ~160 IT-GW by 2030, more than 4.5x the 2025 level. The cover note and Exhibit 1 say 149 IT-GW. The note does not reconcile the two figures.

Site-based method (infrastructure/REIT camp): uses the Aterio project database with completion and delay assumptions. Range is ~134-167 IT-GW by 2030, base 142. It is the most actionable framework for the next few years but loses visibility at longer horizons. Credible GW is estimated at ~35% of the total pipeline.

Incremental growth rate method (industrials/equipment camp): extrapolates the growth in annual capacity additions. Range is 124-242 IT-GW by 2030, base 161. It is highly sensitive to the starting point and growth assumptions and often skews aggressive because equipment orders front-run installed capacity.

Hyperscaler capex method (technology/internet camp): converts capex from Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle into capacity. Base is ~152 IT-GW by 2030, range 115-195. It is the widest of the five because capex is not capacity: spending mix, hardware refresh and disclosure gaps all move the result.
Server-based method (semis camp): built on David Dai's AI server power model, adjusted for the U.S. Base is ~149 IT-GW by 2030, range 137-160. It is hard to align on timing and refresh cycles.

Craft labor method (Chad Dillard): a workforce-availability ceiling rather than a demand forecast. Base is ~142 IT-GW by 2030, range 120-204. It is among the most conservative of the five, along with the site-based method.

Definitions drive much of the spread. IT-GW (critical IT capacity, after a PUE haircut) differs from facility GW (nameplate, used by electrical and power analysts). Bernstein converts with a PUE of 1.3 in 2026, trending down. Equipment orders, facility energization and hardware purchases each occur at different points in the cycle.

Starting point: credible estimates of end-2025 U.S. capacity range from 30 to 80 GW. Bernstein anchors to 35 IT-GW, counting only active data centers in its pipeline data. It says the figure should perhaps be closer to 45 GW but keeps the source historicals so the incremental numbers are not distorted.

Forecasts have been revised up almost uniformly. McKinsey raised its 2030 forecast 258% between 2025 and 2026, BCG 155% and EPRI 99%. Bernstein says its own numbers have also ballooned since its global model early in the year, and that it changed its sourcing and methodology.

Build timelines give some near-term visibility: a facility takes at least 18 months to build, and typically 3+ years of planning, with legislation in TX, PA and NY extending that. Some projects will be delayed or never convert, and some believe hyperscalers are over-ordering and building in a natural failure rate.

Investment stance: Bernstein favors companies with direct exposure to energized capacity growth over those whose outlook depends on the current pace of AI adoption. It describes the market as supply constrained, with new supply often absorbed shortly after delivery.
Stated risk: the greatest risk is concentrated where valuations already assume the most aggressive capacity outcomes materialize without execution challenges or delays.

Hyperscaler capex assumptions (Exhibit 13): total capex of $466B in 2025, $856B in 2026E, $1,166B in 2027E and $1,269B in 2030E. The estimated U.S. share is $642B in 2026E and $951B in 2030E, with 85% allocated to data centers.

sector_views.sector: Data center developers and colocation providers
sector_views.rationale: Demand for AI infrastructure exceeds available capacity in many regions, and new supply is absorbed shortly after delivery.
Multi-year revenue visibility if the base case holds. Equipment orders run ahead of capacity activation.

sector_views.sector: AI infrastructure names priced for the most aggressive capacity outcomes
sector_views.rationale: The greatest risk is where valuations assume the most aggressive capacity outcomes materialize without execution challenges or delays.

risk_factors: Valuations that already assume the most aggressive capacity outcomes materialize without execution challenges or delays.
Projects can be delayed, resized, canceled or replaced for regulatory, construction or business reasons. Not everything at the top of the pipeline funnel will become operational.
Hyperscalers may be over-ordering and building in a natural failure rate on construction projects.
Craft labor shortages, power infrastructure, equipment availability and permitting can cap the pace of construction.
Legislation in TX, PA and NY is extending planning timelines.
Data quality: hyperscalers give no meaningful data on existing capacity, and the market has a long tail of private players, so starting points are uncertain.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: Bernstein average base case U.S. IT-GW rises from 33.7 in 2025 to 149.2 in 2030E.
Exhibit 2: base cases from the five methods converge at 142.3 to 161.0 IT-GW in 2030E. Site-based is 142.3, incremental growth 161.0, hyperscale capex 151.5, server-based 148.6 and craft labor 142.4.
Exhibit 28: distribution of 2025 U.S. installed IT capacity estimates ranges from 23 to 80 GW across sources, with Bernstein at about 34 GW.

tension_points.bull_case: Growth-rate extrapolation reaches a base of 161 IT-GW and a high of 242 IT-GW. The server and capex methods give 149 and 152 IT-GW. Equipment orders and AI compute demand signal faster build-out than project databases show.
tension_points.bear_case: Site-based (base 142 IT-GW) and craft-labor (base 142 IT-GW) approaches are more conservative. Only about 35% of the pipeline is judged credible, projects get delayed or canceled, and labor, power, equipment and permitting can cap deployment.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The report does not give a specific level. It says the greatest risk is where valuations assume the most aggressive capacity outcomes materialize without execution challenges or delays.

theme_stances.key_argument: Demand for AI infrastructure exceeds available capacity, and new supply is absorbed shortly after delivery, supporting a durable build cycle.
theme_stances.evidence: Today's market remains supply constrained, with demand for AI infrastructure exceeding available capacity

theme_stances.key_argument: Skilled labor availability sets a practical ceiling on how much capacity the industry can physically build.
theme_stances.evidence: craft labor may be one of the biggest ceilings limiting data center construction
